title: The workplace at B2: pay, meetings and a diplomatic no
title_target: Finns det något utrymme för en kompromiss?
goal: Negotiate your salary, give critical feedback and turn down a request in the soft, consensus-seeking style of a Swedish workplace.
bekal: you can state a salary claim, argue for it and propose a compromise
you can wrap criticism in the Swedish way: praise, hedge, invite
you can say no without saying *nej* — and decode what Swedish colleagues really mean

notes: **Lönesamtal** (**LÖ-neh-sahm-tahl**) — in most Swedish workplaces, salaries are individual but set inside a **kollektivavtal** (collective agreement) negotiated by the unions. About two in three Swedish employees belong to a union, and **facket** (the union, colloquially) publishes pay statistics by profession, age and region. Turning up with those numbers, as Dian does, is normal and respected.

**Vad har du för löneanspråk?** — *vad … för* is a split question word meaning "what kind of, what": *Vad har du för bil?* (What car do you have?). **Löneanspråk** (**LÖ-neh-ahn-sprohk**), literally "salary claim", is the figure you ask for. Always give it as a monthly gross amount: *i månaden före skatt*.

**…vore rimligt** — *vore* is the formal past subjunctive of *vara* (Unit 13), equal to *skulle vara*. "42,000 would be reasonable" sounds firm but not pushy; *jag vill ha 42 000* would sound like a demand. **Med tanke på** (considering) is one of the complex prepositions from Unit 9.

**Förankra** (**för-AHNK-rah**), literally "to anchor", is a key verb of Swedish working life: to get a decision accepted by everyone affected before it is taken. *Jag behöver förankra det hos ledningen* is not an excuse — it is how decisions are made. It makes Swedish decisions slow to reach but solid once taken.

**Avstämning** (**AHV-stem-ning**) — a check-in, follow-up meeting; the verb is *stämma av* (to check in, align). **Till hösten** means "in the coming fall": *till* + definite season points forward in time.

**Friskvårdsbidrag** (**FRISK-vohds-bee-drahg**) is a tax-free allowance many employers pay for gym cards, swimming, massage or yoga. It is a typical Swedish **förmån** (benefit), along with extra vacation days, a pension top-up (*tjänstepension*) and lunch vouchers.

grammars.title: The conditional as a politeness tool
body: At work, Swedes soften almost every request and claim. The tools are the ones you already know — *skulle*, *vore*, past tense for politeness, and questions instead of commands. What changes at B2 is how systematically you use them.

head: Direct
Softened
What changes
rows: **Finns det möjlighet** att få mer tid?
a question about the situation, not the person

after: **Hade tänkt** is a typically Swedish softener: the pluperfect makes the plan sound tentative, open to change. *Jag hade tänkt gå tidigare idag, om det går bra?* is the perfect way to ask to leave early.

Imperatives are not rude in themselves (*Ta en kaka!*), but at work an imperative about someone's task — *Gör om rapporten* — sounds harsh. Turn it into a question or a *vi*-sentence: *Ska vi titta på rapporten igen?*

notes: **Det finns mycket bra i det … Ett litet [men]** — Dian follows the classic Swedish feedback recipe: something specific and positive first, then the criticism as a question or a possibility (*jag undrar om…*), then an invitation (*vad tror du själv?*). Direct criticism exists in Sweden, but between colleagues of the same rank this soft packaging is the norm.

**Det svider** (**deh SVEE-der**) — *svida* means "to sting, smart" (of a wound, or of words). *Det svider lite att höra* is an honest, slightly self-ironic way to accept criticism. **Synpunkter** (**SÜN-pünk-ter**), literally "view-points", is the neutral word for comments and feedback.

**Tar jag det också, blir kvaliteten lidande** — a condition without *om*: the verb comes first, and the main clause follows after the comma (compare English "Should I take it…"). It is very common in spoken Swedish. **Bli lidande** (**LEE-dahn-deh**) means "to suffer, to be the one that loses out".

**Jag skulle gärna hjälpa till, men…** is the Swedish polite no in its purest form. Notice what Dian does next: she does not stop at no but offers a **conditional yes** (*Om någon annan kan…, kan jag…*). This keeps the consensus mood and puts the decision back where it belongs, with the manager.

**Det brådskar** (**deh BROHS-kahr**) — "it's urgent". An impersonal verb, like *det regnar*: there is no person doing the hurrying. **Från och med** (from and including) is the standard way to say "starting from": *från och med nästa månad*, often shortened to *fr.o.m.* in writing.
**Snyggt hanterat** — *snygg* (good-looking, neat) is used for anything done elegantly: *snyggt jobbat!* (nice work!), *snyggt mål* (a nice goal). The *-t* form works as an adverb.

grammars.title: Feedback and refusals: a phrase kit
body: These phrases carry most of the diplomatic weight in a Swedish workplace. Learn them as whole chunks.

head: Function
Phrase
English
rows: There's a lot that's good in…
En sak jag funderar på är…
One thing I'm thinking about is…
Just nu har jag fullt upp med…
Right now I've got my hands full with…
Can I get back to you on that?

after: **Kan jag återkomma?** is not a hidden no — Swedes mean it, and they expect you to get back. Use it when you need to check your workload or *förankra* something first.

Notice the word order in *Om någon annan kan ta rapporteringen, **kan jag** gå in*: the whole *om*-clause fills the first position, so the verb follows straight after the comma (Unit 1 and 2). A *så* may stand in between: *Om …, så kan jag…* — common and correct in speech.

blocks.text: A Swedish job usually starts with a **provanställning** of up to six months, after which it turns into a **tillsvidareanställning** — literally "employment until further notice", the Swedish word for a permanent contract. Pay is reviewed once a year in the **löneöversyn**, and that is when the *lönesamtal* takes place. A good negotiator comes with facts (statistics, results, new responsibilities) rather than personal needs: *jag har fått mer ansvar* works; *min hyra har gått upp* does not.

blocks.title: Negotiating in Swedish: five rules
items: Name a concrete figure, monthly and before tax: *42 000 i månaden*.
Argue with results and responsibility: *Jag har drivit…*, *Med tanke på…*
Soften the claim, not the number: *…vore rimligt*.
Have a fallback ready: *Finns det utrymme för…?*, *Kan vi titta på andra förmåner?*
Close by summarizing: *Då är vi överens om att…*

blocks.text: A Swedish meeting aims at a decision everyone can live with. The manager often speaks last, the quiet colleague is asked for an opinion, and open conflict is avoided. The flip side: criticism often comes so wrapped up that foreigners miss it entirely. Learn to read the understatement.

head: What they say
What they often mean
rows: Det kanske kan vara värt att titta på.
Jag hör vad du säger, men…
Ska vi ta ett varv till?

blocks.title: Useful meeting phrases
items: *Får jag flika in en sak?* — May I just add something?
*Jag vill bara lyfta en fråga.* — I'd just like to raise an issue.
*Kan vi parkera den frågan?* — Can we park that question?
*Vem tar den?* — Who's taking that one?
*Ska vi runda av?* — Shall we wrap up?
